Saving the Colors of the Sea

In the summer of 2024, Mrs. Chan, a recreational diver from Sai Kung, went snorkeling into the clear waters near Sharp Island expecting to see the vibrant coral she had photographed for years. Instead, she saw large patches of coral turned ghostly white. For Mrs. Chan, coral bleaching was no longer a scientific term in a news report. It had become a painful reality beneath the waters of Hong Kong. Her experience reminds us that coral bleaching is not a distant environmental issue. It is happening here, now, and its consequences affect both nature and people.

Coral reefs are often called the “rainforests of the sea” because Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor, yet support roughly 25% of marine fish and other ocean species. Globally, coral bleaching has reached alarming levels. In 2025, scientists reported that about 84% of the world’s coral reef ecosystems had experienced bleaching stress, making it the most extensive bleaching event ever recorded. Rising ocean temperatures caused by climate change force corals to expel the algae that provide them with food and color, leaving behind pale white skeletons. Although Hong Kong is not famous for coral reefs like Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, it is home to diverse coral communities. Recent reports have shown that coral bleaching has appeared repeatedly in Hong Kong waters, increasing significantly in 2022 and again in 2024.

The most effective solution combines climate action, local coral conservation and innovative reef interventions. First, Hong Kong should scale up artificial reefs and 3D-printed clay reef tiles. Since 1996, Hong Kong has deployed artificial reefs, using sunken vessels and repurposed tires to rebuild habitats and boost fish populations. Currently, 3D-printed terracotta reef tiles are used, with their complex, porous surfaces that help coral fragments anchor securely to regrow. Moreover, this should be paired with nutrient management with coral probiotics to strengthen coral health directly in the ocean. Nutrient management techniques limit excess nitrogen and phosphorus to prevent harmful algal blooms, while coral probiotics introduce beneficial microbes that reshape the coral in situ to help corals withstand heat stress and disease. Together, physical reef tiles and biological treatment can help improve coral survival. Secondly, governments must reduce greenhouse gas emissions by accelerating the use of renewable energy and decreasing dependence on fossil fuels. Since warmer oceans are the primary cause of bleaching, addressing climate change would reduce temperature rise. Lastly, Hong Kong should expand coral monitoring and restoration programs. Marine scientists can identify areas most vulnerable to bleaching and focus conservation efforts there. Coral nurseries, where fragments of healthy coral are grown and later transplanted into damaged reefs, have already shown promise in many parts of the world. Such projects can increase reef resilience and speed up recovery after bleaching.

This solution works because it addresses both the cause and the symptoms of coral bleaching. Global climate policies reduce future warming, while local conservation projects protect reefs that still have a chance to recover. Rather than relying on a single strategy, this approach creates a coordinated response involving governments, scientists, and citizens.

The benefits of protecting coral reefs extend far beyond marine life. Healthy reefs support local fisheries by providing sheltered breeding, feeding, and nursery habitats where commercial fish species grow and replenish stocks. They also strengthen Hong Kong’s tourism sector by drawing divers, snorkelers, and eco-tourists to marine parks like Hoi Ha Wan and Sai Kung. Beyond these gains, reef structures buffer wave energy to reduce coastal erosion and storm damage, ensuring future generations gain a richer biodiversity and healthier oceans. Readers can contribute immediately by reducing their carbon footprint, choosing sustainable seafood, avoiding single-use plastics, and supporting marine conservation organizations.

Mrs. Chan’s dive near the Sharp Island proves that coral bleaching is already reshaping Hong Kong’s waters, yet reefs remain remarkably. With decisive climate action and science- backed restoration today, Hong Kong’s reefs can bloom again. Act now, and future generations will dive into thriving color instead of empty stone.
